dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Cross-border outsourcing: Oversight follows the provider chain
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core proposition that outsourcing does not transfer professional responsibility and materially develops it through scenario-based guidance on provider and intermediary diligence, supervision, confidentiality controls, conflicts, UPL, and context-sensitive disclosure and consent.
qs: The New York law firm retains complete responsibility for the work of the foreign  professional; the firm and cannot abdicate that responsibility in reliance on the fact that the  people conducting the searches hold a law license in the foreign jurisdiction.

st.t: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
st.an: The report supports the synthesis’s core position that outsourcing does not transfer professional responsibility and that billing treatment depends on the nature of the charge and client consent. It requires continuing supervision and recommends advance consent when substantive outsourced work is billed above actual cost plus reasonable overhead, consistent with rejecting undisclosed or duplicative recovery.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Although addressing offshore legal outsourcing rather than AI, the report supports the cluster’s core human-led, selective-deployment logic: delegation does not transfer professional accountability, and substantive work requires informed verification, competent supervision and controls adapted to the task and risk. It does not address AI capability evidence, productivity or labour effects.

kp.k: Offshore outsourcing responds to cost and capacity pressures
kp.d: The report describes offshore legal support rather than AI. It states that law firms and corporate legal departments have used overseas providers for cost savings, faster responses and overflow management, with expansion driven by client pressure for efficiency. Covered tasks include research, drafting, discovery review, patent searches and due diligence. These are contextual assertions, not quantified empirical findings.
qs: Outsourcing has expanded as corporate legal departments and law firms have faced growing pressure from clients to reduce costs and manage operations more efficiently.
conducting legal research, drafting legal memoranda or briefs, reviewing discovery materials, conducting patent searches, performing due diligence, or drafting contracts.

kp.k: Different outsourcing arrangements retain domestic professional responsibilities
kp.d: The report distinguishes intermediary-managed services, direct retention of foreign firms, captive arrangements employing foreign lawyers, and agreements for U.S. legal work to be completed abroad. Providers can include foreign-qualified lawyers without U.S. admission and nonlawyers. In the described direct-support relationship without co-counsel status, the U.S. firm retains full responsibility; later conflict guidance distinguishes co-counsel relationships from temporary staffing arrangements.
qs: the U.S. law firm does not enter into a co-counsel relationship with the foreign law firm, and thus retains full responsibility for the work performed
The individuals performing the services include lawyers admitted to practice in the foreign jurisdiction but not admitted in any U.S. jurisdiction, and non-lawyers.

kp.k: Ethical permission depends on continuing safeguards
kp.d: The Committee presents practical guidance under New York's professional rules, drawing on the New York City Bar's 2006 opinion, ABA Formal Opinion 08-451 and other ethics opinions. It treats outsourcing as conditionally permissible, requiring competence, supervision, confidentiality protection, conflict checks, appropriate billing, disclosure or consent where appropriate, and avoidance of unauthorized practice. This is professional guidance, not an unconditional authorization or evidence of compliance in practice.
qs: This report will cite the New York Rules of Professional Conduct (the “Rules”), adopted as of April 1, 2009.
Although such outsourcing may be ethically permitted, the practitioner would be well advised to identify the lurking ethical issues and consider the guidance described in this paper.
We note that similar considerations apply to domestic outsourcing.

kp.k: Competence requires provider diligence and substantive supervision
kp.d: The report recommends examining intermediary practices and references, foreign credentials and disciplinary regimes, individual references and sample work, communication abilities, firm review practices and insurance. Outsourcing lawyers must possess or acquire sufficient substantive competence, select capable providers and tailor supervision to their training. Remote location, language, time zones and legal-system differences can make effective supervision harder; the report quotes North Carolina guidance against retention when adequate supervision cannot be maintained.
qs: The law firm should interview the intermediary’s managers and employees.
The law firm should obtain and check references for the intermediary
The law firm should also find out whether there is testing or a certification process in the foreign jurisdiction
establish regular communication practices to ensure that the foreign professional has reasonable access to supervising lawyers in the local law firm.

kp.k: Foreign confidentiality regimes require jurisdiction-specific risk assessment
kp.d: The report recommends assessing differences in confidentiality, privilege, government seizure powers and data protection before transmitting client materials overseas. It identifies trade secrets, proprietary information, sealed materials and court orders as reasons for special scrutiny. Where relevant seizure risks exist, it recommends discussion and client consent. Federal prohibitions on disclosure require narrowing the outsourced work or abandoning the arrangement, rather than relying on consent alone.
qs: In addition, federal law may prohibit sending certain information offshore.

If sharing information with a foreign professional is prohibited under federal law, the New York firm must either limit the scope of legal services to be provided offshore to those which would not require sharing information subject to the federal prohibition, or refrain from outsourcing the work.
whether there is any significant risk of seizure of client data under local law

kp.k: Contracts and restricted data access support confidentiality
kp.d: Recommended safeguards include instructing providers about U.S. confidentiality obligations, contractual restrictions extending to subcontractors, provider liability for confidentiality breaches, minimum security standards, breach notification and consideration of encryption. The report also recommends minimizing shared information and, where seizure risks are significant, retaining data on U.S. firm servers with limited access. Captive arrangements, segregated client data and dedicated staff are presented as possible additional precautions, not universal requirements.
qs: Review the outsource and legal service provider’s data security arrangements and impose minimum requirements for data security as a term of contract.
The contract with the outsource provider should also provide for notification to the U.S. lawyer of any breach of the outsource provider’s or legal service provider’s security systems.
Minimize the amount of information about the underlying matter shared with the outsourcing provider

kp.k: Conflict obligations depend on provider relationships and access
kp.d: The report recommends investigating intermediaries' conflict systems and providers' current and former adverse engagements, potentially through questionnaires. Co-counsel relationships require checks consistent with New York rules; where an intermediary resembles a temporary attorney agency without contractual checking responsibility, the New York lawyer remains responsible. Matter-limited access informs the report's treatment of imputation. In its direct foreign-firm research scenario, it states that one professional's conflict disables the entire foreign firm under New York Rule 1.10. Its substantive-service guidance excludes administrative providers from conflict inquiries.
qs: the New York lawyer remains fully responsible for the conflict check.
the foreign professional should not be able to access information regarding other clients of the New York lawyer
if any professional at Lawyers ‘R’ Us would be conflicted from working on the matter, then all professionals at the firm are vicariously disabled from the representation.

kp.k: Disclosure and consent reflect substance, risk and billing
kp.d: The report distinguishes the 2006 opinion's rejection of automatic disclosure for every offshore support assignment from its own recommendation that disclosure be the rule for substantive legal outsourcing. Advance consent is required when client confidences are shared and recommended when billing exceeds actual cost plus reasonably allocated overhead. Otherwise, consent depends on the significance and risk of the provider's role, with consent generally recommended and written documentation advised. The direct research-and-brief-writing scenario calls for advance consent because the work is substantive.
qs: client disclosure should be the rule whenever, as in this scenario, legal
With respect to those clients whose confidences will be shared, advance consent must be obtained.
the actual cost (together with a reasonable allocation of overhead charges associated with the work)
Generally, consent is recommended.
Assuming client consent is advisable, such consent should be formalized in a writing to avoid any confusion later.

kp.k: Supervision prevents delegation from becoming unauthorized practice
kp.d: Invoking New York Rule 5.5, the report explains that foreign licensure does not remove the domestic lawyer's responsibility for outsourced U.S. legal support. The lawyer must determine the appropriate scope, retain professional judgment and review completed work. Research and drafting may be delegated under adequate supervision, but the domestic firm cannot rely on overseas credentials as a substitute for oversight.
qs: A lawyer shall not aid a non-lawyer in the unauthorized practice of law.

retain complete responsibility for the work of the foreign professional, use his or her professional skill and judgment to set the appropriate scope for the foreign professional’s work, and then vet this work to ensure its quality.
adequate supervision, which requires advance consideration of the work that needs to be done and review of the work after it has been performed.

kp.d: Four hypothetical scenarios apply the framework to patent searches, research and brief writing, transactional due diligence, and vendor contracts. Research supervision includes ongoing communication and local checking as necessary; sensitive due diligence may warrant additional background investigation, on-site observation or spot-checking. Contract drafting requires relevant jurisdictional knowledge within the provider or supervising team. In-house departments bear comparable oversight obligations; where the company itself outsources, the report treats separate client disclosure and consent as inapplicable while recommending that legal inform the business unit.
qs: check the research locally to the extent necessary to ensure confidence in the work product.
spot-check the review locally or in the foreign location.

the law department should confirm that either the firm has professionals who are familiar with the laws governing the vendor contracts in the relevant jurisdictions, or that the local lawyers who will supervise the work are familiar with the relevant laws and will be able to provide adequate supervision.
Nevertheless, it behooves the in-house legal department to inform the business unit of its outsourcing plans.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report makes no AI claims. In its own domain of offshore legal outsourcing, the Committee claims that outsourcing has delivered cost savings, faster responses and capacity flexibility, and has expanded under client cost pressure.
pts.d: The August 2009 report by the New York City Bar's Committee on Professional Responsibility concerns delegation to overseas human lawyers and nonlawyers, not automation. It describes existing outsourcing practices rather than forecasting AI adoption or displacement. Its substantive claim is that law firms and corporate legal departments can outsource legal support, including research, drafting, discovery review and due diligence, while retaining professional responsibility. These are outsourcing claims, not evidence of AI's effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The report relies on professional ethics authorities and illustrative scenarios; it does not quantify outsourcing's commercial benefits or growth.
pts.d: The commercial-benefits statement cites an August 5, 2008 Strafford teleconference on ethical risks of offshore outsourcing. No cost comparisons, adoption statistics or response-time measurements are supplied. The Committee's guidance draws on New York City Opinion 2006-3, ABA Formal Opinion 08-451, other state and local ethics opinions, and New York's professional conduct rules. Cases concerning privilege and foreign law support its confidentiality discussion, not its commercial-benefits claims. Its four outsourcing scenarios are illustrations, not reported empirical case studies. Quoted conclusions from other ethics committees are supporting authorities rather than independent findings by this Committee.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe practices existing by August 2009; outsourcing's permissibility is conditional on competent supervision and other ethical safeguards.
pts.d: The report refers to outsourcing over 'several years' and supplies no numerical forecast or future deadline. Its New York rules discussion uses the rules adopted as of April 1, 2009. Conditions include competent selection and supervision, protection of confidential information, conflict checks, appropriate billing, disclosure and consent where warranted, and avoidance of assisting unauthorized practice. Foreign legal training, geographical distance, time differences and communication barriers can complicate supervision. Federal restrictions may require limiting or abandoning offshore work. Informed consent is required for sharing client confidences; broader consent recommendations depend on the work's substance and risk. These are historical statements of the report's guidance, not assertions about current law.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are outsourcing law firms and corporate legal departments, offshore human service providers and intermediaries, and clients whose work and information are delegated.
pts.d: Law firms and corporate legal departments receive the claimed operational benefits but retain oversight obligations. Foreign law firms, legal support businesses, foreign-qualified lawyers and nonlawyers perform delegated substantive work; intermediaries may recruit, credential and manage them. Clients face confidentiality, privilege and service-quality risks, with disclosure and consent protections. Corporate legal departments act on the buyer side, and the report recommends informing the relevant business unit when they outsource. The report offers no claims about AI vendors, entry-level job losses, changes to firm staffing structures or access to justice.
